title: New quantum chip taps into weird quasiparticles to get qubits to communicate over long distances
source_used: Live Science; University of Warwick press release read as a cross-check
key_facts: Live Science (5 Oct 2026): researchers have developed a new interconnected architecture for quantum computing chips that could pave the way for machines with over a million qubits.
The study was published on 15 Jun in APL Quantum (the citation line gives 2026); first author Maksym Myronov is an associate professor at the University of Warwick, UK.
Problem: in leading quantum processors, qubits struggle to share quantum information unless they are immediate neighbours.

Idea: Quantum Phononic Links (QPLs) use phonons, quasiparticles that carry vibration energy, to pass information between distant qubits; conventional options such as surface acoustic waves need complex designs and extra hardware.
Best fit: semiconductor hole spin qubits in compressively strained germanium on silicon (cs-GoS), a thin germanium layer on silicon.
Live Science says the team created a prototype QPU and used QPLs to link qubits less than a micrometre apart and up to 300 mm (11.8 inches) apart.

[Warwick release, read separately] calls the work 'a new concept' and says the researchers 'show that, in principle', quantum information could be transferred between qubits across a chip up to 300 mm in diameter; it describes no built device.
[Earlier coverage] The Warwick release was covered by Phys.org (27 Jul 2026) and Quantum Zeitgeist (28 Jul 2026, 'proposing a new communication system'), then by other outlets into August.
quote_evidence: In a study published June 15 in the journal APL Quantum, scientists aimed to resolve a huge problem with the leading quantum processing units (QPUs): Qubits struggle to communicate and share quantum information with each other if they aren't immediate neighbors.

To demonstrate this technology, they created a prototype QPU consisting of silicon with a thin germanium crystal layer, a specialized material they called compressively strained germanium on silicon (cs-GoS).

[Warwick release] A new concept from Warwick researchers could help solve one of the biggest challenges to building large-scale quantum computers: enabling communication between vast numbers of quantum bits (qubits) over long distances across a single chip.
why_it_matters_hint: A way to link distant qubits on one chip addresses one of the open problems in building quantum computers with very many qubits.
event_date: Paper published 15 Jun 2026 (APL Quantum); Warwick release first covered 27 Jul 2026; Live Science piece dated 5 Oct 2026.
notes: Old news re-dated into the window: the paper is from 15 Jun 2026 and the Warwick release was covered by Phys.org on 27 Jul, Quantum Zeitgeist on 28 Jul, Bisinfotech on 29 Jul, The Brighter Side of News on 3 Aug and All About Circuits on 18 Aug 2026; Live Science adds no new result. Live Science says a prototype QPU was created, whereas Warwick's release and Quantum Zeitgeist describe a concept shown 'in principle'; the entry follows the more cautious wording. The year of the study is taken from the citation line (APL Quantum 3(2), 2026). The page text starts with subscription boilerplate; only the article body was used.
